title: Bully Sticks vs Antlers: Picking a Chew That Matches How Your Dog Chews
description: Bully sticks are fully consumable and softer, while antlers are extremely hard and meant to last much longer. Here's how to match either one to your dog's actual chewing strength instead of picking based on what's popular.
quick_answer: Bully sticks are a single-ingredient, fully digestible chew that softens as your dog works through it, making them a good everyday option that gets fully consumed over time. Antlers are extremely hard, don't get consumed the same way, and are built to last much longer, but that hardness carries a real risk of tooth fracture for aggressive chewers. If you want a chew your dog finishes and you replace regularly, bully sticks fit better. If you want something that lasts a long time and your dog chews moderately rather than aggressively, an antler can work, but it's worth understanding the tooth-fracture risk before choosing one for a strong chewer.
card_summary: One gets fully eaten. The other barely wears down. The right choice depends on how hard your dog actually bites.

faqs.question: Are antlers safe for dogs?
faqs.answer: They can be, but their hardness carries a real risk of cracking teeth, especially for dogs that chew aggressively or bite down hard rather than gnawing gradually. Moderate chewers tend to handle antlers more safely than dogs that apply heavy, sustained bite force.

faqs.question: Why do bully sticks have a smell?
faqs.answer: It comes from the natural drying process used to make them, and the intensity varies by brand and processing method. Some bully sticks are processed specifically to reduce odor, while others retain more of the natural smell.

faqs.question: Which lasts longer, a bully stick or an antler?
faqs.answer: Antlers generally last significantly longer, since they're extremely hard and don't break down the way a bully stick does through normal chewing. A bully stick is meant to be fully consumed over time, while an antler is built to withstand chewing without disappearing the same way.

faqs.question: Can puppies have bully sticks or antlers?
faqs.answer: Bully sticks are generally considered appropriate for puppies in proper sizes, since they soften as a dog works through them. Antlers are harder to recommend broadly for puppies, since their teeth are still developing and the extreme hardness carries more risk during that stage.

body:
## What's the actual difference between these two chews?

One gets eaten. The other doesn't, really.

A bully stick is a single-ingredient chew, typically made from dried beef muscle, that softens gradually as your dog works through it. Over time, your dog actually consumes the whole thing, which means you're replacing it regularly as part of a normal routine.

An antler is a naturally shed deer or elk antler, extremely hard, and built to withstand chewing without breaking down much at all. Your dog gnaws on it, but doesn't really consume it the way they do a bully stick. That's the entire tradeoff in a nutshell: consumable and softer, versus long-lasting and much harder.

## Why does hardness actually matter here?

Because extreme hardness carries a real risk for aggressive chewers.

A dog that chews moderately, working an item around with steady pressure, tends to handle a hard antler reasonably well. A dog that bites down hard and applies a lot of sustained force is at real risk of fracturing a tooth against something as hard as an antler. That risk doesn't really exist with a bully stick, since it softens as your dog works through it instead of staying rigid.

If you're not sure how hard your dog actually bites, it's worth watching them with a chew you're already comfortable with before introducing something as hard as an antler.

## When does a bully stick make the most sense?

For everyday chewing where you want something that gets fully used and replaced regularly.

Bully sticks work well as a routine chew, something your dog finishes over a session or two, rather than an item that sits around indefinitely. They're also generally considered a safer starting point for puppies or dogs you're still getting to know as chewers, since the softening reduces the hardness-related risk that comes with something like an antler.

## When does an antler make more sense?

For a moderate chewer who wants something that lasts a long time without needing frequent replacement.

If your dog gnaws steadily rather than biting down hard and aggressively, an antler can be a long-lasting option that doesn't need to be replaced nearly as often as a consumable chew. The upfront cost is often higher, but the lifespan can offset that if your dog uses it the way it's intended.

## Does the smell of a bully stick matter for choosing one?

It's a real consideration, but it varies by brand and processing method. Some bully sticks have a noticeably stronger smell than others, depending on how they're dried and processed. If odor is a concern, it's worth checking how a specific product is processed rather than assuming all bully sticks smell the same.

## Can I give my dog both types of chews?

Yes, and many owners do, just for different purposes. A bully stick as a regular, consumable chew during the week, and an antler as a longer-lasting option for a dog that chews moderately and benefits from something that doesn't need frequent replacing.

## Should I supervise either type of chew?

Supervision is worth it for both, but for different reasons. With a bully stick, the concern is mostly about a dog swallowing a piece that's gotten too small to chew safely. With an antler, the concern shifts toward hardness-related tooth issues, especially with dogs that bite down aggressively rather than gnawing.

## The bottom line

A bully stick and an antler aren't really competing for the same job. One is a consumable, everyday chew. The other is a long-lasting, much harder option that comes with a real tradeoff in tooth-fracture risk for strong chewers.

Know how your dog actually chews before picking based on lifespan alone.
